Lord ikaconsdeld he. appealed to the country, and she country is responding to the appeal with an emphasis declering We condemnation of his liovernment, and iM de- termination to efface it. The Conservative majority has already ceased to exist, and Lord Beaconefield's administra- tion has practically perished with it, though formally it lives for 11 lew sc.eks longer. llte C'onservative majority was the prop upon which Lord Beacons:kill rested. The circum- stances in which this nmnitestation of opinion in taking place give it a significance airman unique in political struggles. The neCon is not votir.g under the ineuence of passion, but coolly nod deliberately, and Lord Bexons- field'e policy is oondemne,l all along the line. It is certain now that the new House of Commons will contain a lAberal majority ; ,ind it is the business of those timid Liberals who profess above all things to dread a weak Liberal majority to do their lest to make it, and the fiovernment which will spritig from it, strong. Lord Beaconsfield's Administration will either perish by voluntary resignation, re in ISBS, before the meeting of Par- , Hameln, or will In driven from once by a rote of center. limmediately after the House of Commons has been organized. The point which will be determined by the oleeti.ne which have mill to take place in South-West Len- j eashire, the divisions of Cheshire, and other districts, will be the relative strength of tbe Liberal majority, AOli the efficiency depending upon that strength of the coming ; Liberal Administration. Now that its existence is assured, it is the interest and duty of all section@ of the Liberal party to make it

as strong as possible, in. of casual allies and potent enough Ia reoommend its measures to the acquiemence of the limme of 1.01,111. The (1,91i0114 roldoir ire properly farmer. ques- tions -..he land laws, tire dz,ine laws. the mcurity of the tenant's capital from prralato.y landlords, and of his crops from wild aninial--are .ure to eugage the Ileum of Corn. ! mons under • Liberal Administration. It is the dear : interest of the tetatnt farmers el England to strengthee that Liberal majority, on the force and unity of which the acceptance be the Lord. of measures which hare passed the Commons will very largely depend. The eeccess which has bees gained in the English burougl nice remain for . carrying the war into the English cannel, even into such of them as Lave not yet been chaPer.ded. A Liberal Ministry being now • thing of the twat future. the farmers must see the policy and necessity of gis.nd it the strength which is needful if it iA to do tient juatee. Edmunds, Wakefirld,Brecon, Petersfield, Kye, and other pladee. Tory- ism has been slain • hip and thigh." Leeds has decided most significantly in fevour of the Liberal programme. Mr. Gladstone will probably not require the seat the Liberals of Leeds have so handsomely provided for him in his absence but his return attic. head of the poll, with Mr. Barran in the second place, is something mom than • gain of a neat. The Liberal poll in Leedeis so large that • simple division sum will show IL:, 0,- Conservative, Mr. Jackson, who iA ten thounned 1.,: :hr sewed Liberal, only holds that place by i ~hearance el hie opranents. There has been a decline of Coneervatism in Leols. Al Chester there is ne equally remarkable Liberal wee... In those districts whore elections have yet to take place, the Liberal voter. must .incentrate their voter on the candi- dates mom likely to succeed, and :hue defeat the Conserva- tive, who hope to idofit by their division. If the Idberala will vote for the candidates of the united party, the Lancashire and Cheshire ~.ivisirng will said to the Liberal gains. Warr ington has an opportunity to-iLy to return to its old Liberal traditions. and there seems every reason to expect that it will do so.

Both political parties in St. Helens continue to be active, and during this wuk meetings have been held or various ports of the town. tlnTnnnotovevenongntnttgofLotodls was hold in the Old Mill, Liverpool-road, Eccleston, presided once by Mr. B. Pilkington, who was supported on the plat- form hy Alderman Johnson (the mayor), the Rev. 11. J. Weatherhead, Messrs. It. L. Riley, and H. Loren. Amongst the audience were Major Pilkin,gton, Dr. Ricketts, ND. Thos. , Brown, he. The CHAIRMAI, after referring to the importance of the crisis through which they were passing, pnceederl to non-! train the legislation of the Liberal Government with that of the Consvvative Governmeut. He said that Sir. Cross, at the Volunteer Hall, took the entire credit for all sorts of do nestle legislation, but to take credit for what he had done was to take credit for very little. (Fleas. hear.) Mr. Crane took the credit of passing the Factory Acts Consolidation Act. These Acts extended front 1833. Mr. Cross said that they had to look to him and the Government for pusing the Act of 1878. The facts of the case were these he came across in looking into this quution was that of 1833, pawed by a Liberal Governmem; in 1849 a bill for the bctter inspection of collieries was introduced hy two Liberals, and carried ho' a Liberal Government. In 1850 a bill was introduced to pro- tect miners, liut Lord Beaconsfield pretested against it. In 185) Lord Ashley, a Liberal nobleman—(cheere)—brought forward the Factory Act Bill, and it was adopted by the Liberal Government. In 18.53 the Liberals again amended those laws, and the Liberal member for Bolton intraluced the bill. In 1883,18112, and 1864 lord Palmerston int,- ducal bills extended an I amended the Acta ; and in 1871 Om Liberals pissed bills oxtentling the Acts again. Mr. Cross hod told them that he was the great Home Secretary ! What wai the grand measure It, floated before their eyes? It was a number of Acts put together, and Mr. Cross claimed credit for that. A schoolmairter might jut a well eat', "I am the father of all these children." (Laughter.) h wag one of the grutest misrepreeentations ever made, and could only he made by a sham minister—(cheers)—whose only excellence was that he could pus sham legislation hardly worth the paper written upon. He claiined credit for pare. ing the Criminal Law Amendment Act, but the question was kept before Parliament by Mr. Mundella, Mr. Eustace Smith, and other Liberals, and were paned with an important amendment made by Mr. Lowe. Referring to the Employers' and Worktnen'e Act, ivhich prevented the penalty of impri- sonment, he Said that Mr. Cross claimed credit for that very thing. But that bill was moved by Mr. Mundella, and supported by other Liberals, tel opposed by Mr. Cross in the first instance, but afterwards adopted it, yet there Wan I. credit due to him. Them was another bill—The Merchants' Shipping Act, which protected the British seoman. It was introduced by Mr. Plimsoll, and supported by all good Liberal.; and it it had not been for Mr. Plitnsoll and the Liberals that bill would never have been hued c.f. (Cheers.) Mr. Cross was actually taking feathers out of other birds and sticking them in ins Or. tail. (Loud laughter.) The speaker des- cribed the Probate Duties Act as close legislation. and said that great landowners and uuntry gentlemen were not touched by that LW. It was a bill which touched the pockets of workingmen who rise eqt arid build cottages, and shopkeepers and othersof the same clue. He described the Artisans' Dwellings Act ae a great mess; and he did not believe any'uly hut Mr. Cross could have made such a mem of it. That Bill was not created by Mr. Cross, it was Mr. Torrens who brought line some years ago, And 1 woefully in the pigeon holes of the Liberal Goverment when Mr. Crou Wok it up. 11 01,1 Liberal Government had been in power they would have made it a success, but Mr. Crow roads., horrid huh of it, nod then says, "Isn't it a splendid thing." (Laughter.) It was a grave national disaster to have twelve such men at the hud of affairs as the late Cabinet. (A Voice 1 There's only one.") Ile was quite right, the tact woe tlmt Lord Beaconsfield had got the length of the foot of every m.in in the Cabinet at present and thou whom he could not get the length of their feet he got them oat. And unless they got Lord Beaconelield out they would spend millions of English money in increasing our national disaster. (Applausc.) Mr. RtLey, it the course of v,p able speech, referred to the manifesto of Lord Beaconsfield, in which herald, "That there were seine who cholleuged the expeliency of the impedel character of the rulm ;" and said the Liberals did not challenge the cliaracter of the realtn, but the character Of , Imperialism. It svas too rouch of the hoperialism of the Continent which in France had bred Communists, in Russia Nihiliate, in England patriots; but if another term nt •Itice was accorded to the Conservative party it might breed Republicans, it might breed Revolutionists. (Applause.) Speaking in reference to the Agricultural Holdings Act, the speaker said that at Newton, the other day, Colonel Blackburne mid "it would not do him any harm," but he (the speaker) wanted the experience of the tenants. (Cheers.) He ridiculed the statement of Colonel Blackburne, made at Newton, "that the first question that would be raised if the liberals came into power would be the disestablishment of , the English Church." He was not one who believed, at present, in the exp.liency of the disestablishment of the . Church, but the but friends to the Church would be those who rent to Parliament those who would remove some of

He thought that a political alphabet might he constructed which would enumerate the doings of the Tory Govwnmenr. With respect to the five vowels, he thought that by the concluding three—! 0 0— the Government were tolerably well represented. Having ! disposed of the vowels A, Afghanistan; E, East I. The Tories said that if the Lowe of Primogeniture and Entail were abolishsl it would do away with all the oh! : families—and Lord John Manners once said trade and commerce die, but spare,o,spareour old nobility." j (Laughter.) The presumption f the ItiVr at present was that if a man died, all that he had would go to his eldeet sot The Liberals thought that the presumption ought to be the , other way. and that when a man died all his property would , be shared and aliared alike—the widow, of course, fast pro. vidwl for—amongst his ohildren. (Applauee.) The speaker here quoted from a speech by Mr. (fright, in which that gentleman related a story of an industrious man who had acquired and saysl a considerable amount of money, helped by hie three daughters. The man dying, the money went to the eon, who made off with it, leaving the daughters, who had helpsl to accumulate the earnings, poooilvrum the eon in course of time becoming as poor as his sisters by Isis own misconduct. (Shame.) To prevent these hardships the Liberals say that one of the first acts nmet be to reform the Law of Primogeniture. ;Applause.) He said their chairman represented the manufacturer. of St. Helene and he represented the shopkeepers, and it was. very gOOti reprermtaive meeting. Ile Raked front the ex- ' perience of the It six years. if they were satisfied. ["No."] There had been reducing of wages time after time. and the colliers had gone home with twelve or fourteen shillings a week—C" Shame I—to support their wives and families. When he went to Wigan and Kew 200 wagons of coal and no customers, and the men asked him when trade was going to improve, he said to them: "Look at these wagons ; do you think it probable they would lw standing here if they could be dispowl of ?" The men replied "The workingmen had sent the Conservative members of Wigan to Parliament, but wait until the day of election comes." [Loud cheers.] He hoped that the colliers of Wigan would do their doty. l]Flear, hear.] He saw it stated by Mr. Pickard, the colliers' agent, and he read it with shame,that the large colliery proprietors of Wiper had resolved, for the purpose of influencing-their men, to march them hi a hody lathe poll. It was a diegrace they could not exercise their opinions as well as their em- ployers. [Applause.] They might talk about Mr. Glad- stone—pond cheersi—but what had Mr. Gladstone done for them? During the tittle Mr. Gladstone was in power things were quite different ; instead of wages going down month by month, they seem being raised, and all going on in a pros- perous manner. [Hear. hear.] He asked three who it was who supported Daniel O'Connell in obtaining Catholic emancipation. The Literate pminised they woutd do justice to Ireland. and he hoped on the day of election there would not be an Liebman in England but would go in atrongly for the Liberal party. Let them unite like their forefathers, and like them unfurl the banner upon which were the words "Peace, Retrenchment. and Reform,- and under tie cc banner walk to vietory. [Applause.] Mr. Tenets littown, Wesleyan schoolmaster, seconded the resolution, end in the coarse of his remarks said that the Wesleyans about Present wanted some baiting land for a Weeloyan chapel. Col. Blackburne was interviewed. but, no attached was he to the "Church es by law eatablished." that Ile would not let them hare it, but the late Lord IXrhy, Tory though he was, came to the rescue, and let them have some land at a very cheap rate. [Applause.] Speaking of of the Seats Bill, lee mid that Mr. Cross, in being willing to honour a borough like' Accrington, allowed that he was capalde of doing o very dirty trick. Accrington would have sent a Liberal to Parliament. and Lord Hartington, in con- sego, nee, would have been depreverl of the Accrington votes; lett as Mr. Cross, who wet" Lancashire born and Lancashire bred, strong in the arm anti long in the head"—[laughter]— ought to have ransacked that long head of his, and given to Southport and St. Helens two of the vacant NSIA. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman. The resolutions Were carried unanimonsly.

INSTRUCTIONS TO VOTERS. How TO MARK TILE BALLOT PAPER. Ost going into the polling booth, the Returning Officer will a& your name. lie will then look for your same on the register, and write year number the counterfoil. This is est in order t, god out hoer you vote, but to prevent 'Mother titan coming in and voting in your name, and as a cheek upon illegal vote. The Returning Officer will then give • TOO shallot paper. Take it aml mark it in the place pro- vided with • simple X. If you inake env other nark than a airsple X opposite the candidates for whom you vote, your ballot paper wiH be spoiled and vour vote will be throw. away. Take care that you make o simple X. Ballot papers, are sometimes rejected if you make a X with only one leg (Y), or if you put two crosses inatead el one—X X. Any mark by which the ballot pep, can be identified spoils the vote. It is a common Tory dodge to say that the ballot is not secret, but that is ABSOLUTIO, CAL.. The writing f the voter's number on the counterfoil of the ballot patur •..'y affords an opportunity of detecting setae given disqmslitied persons, or the person. elect of tool or absent clew, and the fact that they are disqualiliad, or absent, er dead mnet be proved before the ballot paper is looked at. If an elector icon the register his ballot paper will never be exatnined. even although he m-,y be legally lisqualitied either by having re- ceived parochial relief or is worne other way. The Register, so WOO entoblish,tl by the Petersfield Case in 1874, is condo- cc to tilc right of all to Vfiti, whose names are inscribed opal it, ca.ts they are women, convicted felons, tioket-of- leave men, aliens, policescen, idiots, hin.stics, and infants Sod only inn neon, elector is proved to belong to one of these sategories ie there any chance of his vote being identified. His number on the counterfoil simply shows that he has voted. It does not chow bow Ise has voted, eel it must first be proved that he is not qualified to vote before the number on the counterfoil can be compared with the number on the ballot paper, and his vote aseerMined. When bribery and treating is moved, the 2511, ssction of the Ballot Act merely requires that the poll of the candidate shall be reduced by as many votes as it ean be proved that he has corrupted without any scrutiny of the ballot papers. Voters may rely upon it that not in one case out of a thousand is there the remotest chance of oeerotiey; and if they are on the resister, and are neither peers, convicts, aliens, lunatics, infanta, or policemen, there is not one chance in a that their votes will ever be ascerndned. The counterfoils show nothing without the ballot ropers; the ballot papers show nothing without the counterfoils. As soon as the poll closes the counterfoils are sealed up. If all the ballot papers are thrown into the street after being counted no one ceuld bell from them how anyone voted without comparing them with the counterfoils, which are carefully sealed up and swot to London. The experience of millions of electors, of both peaks, is that the Becurr ABSOLUTELY ncerr.

WHO BUILT SH I AN]) WHO SQUAN- DERED PUBLIC MONEY. Mr. Grethen, speaking at a meeting at Thirsk the other night, referred to the two Mutes which it was being at- tempted to decide the election upon—the foreign policy and the trial] question. He denied that the Liberal party would be coerced by Mr. Parnell, but asserted that they would not be coerced by the (lnsereatives irl,ll doing justice to Ire- land for fear of its being iinputed to unworthy motives. Turning to th• question of who had made matt wars, he rid as the Liberals during the last fifty years halt been in effice far longer than their opponents, it watt not unnatural II they had, according to the principles of proportion, made more wars. But was it fair to hold Mr. Gladstone res., Bible for wars which took place when he held ivory small office comparatively. Since Mr. Gladstone became leader In She House of Commons there Imd been four wars--the Asharee, Abyssinian, dnlrt, and the Afghan wars. Only the Ashantee war had fallen to the lot of the Liberal party. The Liberal pule are prepared, though with the deepest 'egret, to fight when it is absolutely necessary, and when income on the rigid side and in the right cause. Be continued First they charge us with never making wit. then they my we are no chicken-hearted that, if we are returned to power, Russia will gobble up the whole of Weetern Europe. (Laughter.) Are not the natiooe on the Continent tired of this race between military empires, which Inas crushed out the prosperity of their people, is taking eons from every family, and haying hmvy hand upon the wage-earning clam? Cheers.) Are we to think there too learning desire for war bi Europe, which only the peaceful language of Lord Salisbury is able to assuage? I think set; nor do l think that it we came into power the peace of Europe would Ore one whit thrmtened. (Cheers.) The true reendeney of England must be secured at all hitaatde, nod! Shut we shall gain by standing fast on the linom of our tra- Clio.' policy—by respecting treatim, by apholdlng inter- ealional morality, by marehalling our moral end our mate- . Mal forme on the right side. The ascendency of England Elea be maintained. 'fa maintain it we require mi efficient ray. (Cheers.l I will tell you one of the motives that ! indeeed Inch. accept the invimtion to come over to Thereto' The net election was woo by oue vote. A friend told me rat he had seen an elector who atid he had votod in favour ef the Cones,:dive. because Mr. tilatistone had sold all the I tripe of the navy. (Laughter.) I mid to myself I can put that right if Igo over to Think. We did not sell al the rips. Of all that mighty tier which hi. 'men maintaining NO ascendency of England in the Mediterranmn, at Con- waminopte, during the last three years—eyery single ✓ip, with one exception, was built and tillialCd by the ▪ Hera' (lovernment. (Cheers.) On no subject has there been more mistake and more exaggeration than on this. We did not sell all the ships What were sold were some vetted ships, totally out of the present finn of warfare, that were cumbering the docks, but no single fighting ship of say value ww, or could have been, mcriticed in such a man- ner. (Cheers.) What did we do, when we were in office, r to real fighting ships? During the live years of our office we built (12,600 too,, of bonclad shipping ; Iluring the lee yearsof the Conservative Government they bnilt 49,700. We [milt, in other wonbt, 13,000 tons more of ironelade than the Conservatives, who declare WC are always neglecting the Altercate of the navy. Of unarmoured and the unregistered di its they built more than we did. We built 33,700, and they built 45,100 turn', but if you add the two together, we, to the Oct years, built 90,300 t 0,,, of shipping, while they , built 94,800, or nearly 2,000 lons less. We have built more rips than they, yet they reproach us with having neglected the interests of the navy. True, they have spent more money ; but they have not built more ships. I Loud cheers.) There I acknowledge our inferior capacity. We rent on the ehipbeilding and store not,. £13,285,000; they writ during the mete period £20,270.000. That is 8),760,00) more, though they built infinitely leas ironclad tonnage, and had the further advantage that while we were in office priest were 10 per cent. higher. Spreading that over a terlll of years, it would make a difference of £1,400,000 ; add to that the £6,700,11111,and our Conservative friends Imve spent 0,000,000.10ne on the navy than we, while we built 2.0fe0 tone more shipping. (Cheers., They hone spent, no doubt. a ounsiderable portion of that sum in rerwiring ships, and a great portion of that money was more or less frittered away. But, primp, it will he said, "You neglected the inen in the navy." lan the contrary, they have not added one sin- gle man to the fleet during their six years, but have reduced the marines by 1,000 ; and then they say we were inade- quate in our preparations. They ilaVe enlisted fewer boys ; but, in breed tone., it may Is. said tlmt, as regards manning the navy, their policy is precisely the tome as ours, and all these charge, against us have resolved themsolvm into wiending a few more huedred thousand pounds in repairs. When we first went out of office, the charge was made that we 0111 V had a phantom fleet, and sowed my friends were eurpri;ed I did not at once jump up and answer that 'knack but I confine,' myself to toying, "Stand by your words, and I, though in bpposition, will assist you in obtaining any additiond money, even to a million, which you may require for he ther naval expenditore,” and I was able to l time c got the tmh I ino7:s",*r,..f kb;,.:1,7„ need only take one ie order to incr.., the navy, if they bad shorn. Mr. SLATER, Witten Lodge, read a paper entitle.' "Thoughts on the Land Laws and some suggested amend- ments," The epeaker disapproved of the law of entail and primogeniture, and snggested changes in the law by which, for instance, • landowner who waa unable to drain his Lind except by carrying works outside his own property might be enabled, under proper regula- tions to have that privilege. The law of settlement copyhold property, church lands, the Enclosure Act, the principle of compulsion, the game laws, and lastly the rela- tion between landlord and tenant were dealt with in an able and exhaustive manner. Referring to copyholds Mr. Slater says :—.` A capyhold or customary freehold belongs to or is A portion of some manor. It is a romnant of feudalism. The lord of the manor is the nominal owner, and yet in most case, his only claim is a rent of a few psnce per acre and an absolute cLim for the performance of seine feudal service. The copyholder Ainnot sell a bit of land for a cottage with- out the consent of his loot The estate must first be surren- dered to tbe hod and then the buyer is adtnitted the owner Icy the lord of the ',limner. 13 such a case a sort of double conveyance is required, besides a lot of formalitiee, and the costa are generally fearful. The copyhold owner cannot even grant a lease to a tenant for more than one ymrwithout the lord's consent, and he is restrained in sundry ways and in a manner which is at variance with the rights of real ownership. We have a number of copyhold mmtes in thin country; and any gentleman who has made himself ac- quainted with thetn will be mire to Cottle to the concl union that their continuance is an intolerable and needless vem- tion and oppression, and that their absolute enfranchisetnent Ca pressing necessity. I would eweep away by one general not the very existence of estates in copyhold such as we hnn e in Cheshire, and I would make it compulsory to grant an estate in fee to every applicant on the lord of the manor being paid the proper and full value of all his feudal mother I rights. This one not would do no wrong to anybody, and it , would liberate and bring into hand a nutnber of small mtates In this country, and it would enable All the owners of copy. hold to sell or team their property as they may think fit.” I With reference to the Game Uwe the emayist Pant there is scarcely a law on the Statute Book which hoe been morel severely ctiticised It moot we wish (far from It) to inter- fere with that love of field sport which is of vital iinportance ' in assisting to unbend the minds of thousands of gentlemen ' in this country who, from the nature of their avocation, are heavily oppremed with brain work. We have no wish to limit their country enjoyment or their field recreation, and yet on the other hand yearn told that the Game Laws make poachers poachers make drunkards, and drunkards makes thieves. Poaching Is the mbool where many thieve, take their first lessons. It is the training ground where they take their first exercise. If we loch at the Game Lows from this point, it seems to be largely answerable for much of the de- moralization and criminality WiliCh we have. One thing semon to be certain, that we shall never annihilate the poachers m long asthey find profitable employment. The' question is, what can we do? Personally, I am of opinion 1 that a Trmpass Act. if well drawn and made sufficiently exact, would meet the entire case. We might bane “the common trespass," the wilful and I malicious trespee,"" and the aggravated trespam." Them might be included in this last count all cases of gangs of persons wandering about in search of prey, and all cams of prowling about, on enclosed land, in the night. A law of tilia sort might he made to meet the whole mac, and it would relieve the tee itmlf and its administrators from much , odium. I think we shall do right in very respectfully cont. mending this subject to the very careful consideration of all I gentlemen whose voice can be heard in the legislative councils of this nation, Supposing that a trespass bred this nature were substituted for the prment Game Law it would not necessarily lessen the quantity of (none, nor would it he less necessary to the out shooting licenses, and , persons shooting and sporting on their own land might be required to take out certitimtes We often hear of very strong objection to landlords letting the shooting upon their manors to sporting gentlemen. I thirk it would put a litnn ; to these complaints, and would be far more satisfactory if , the tenant had the option of renting the game on his own ! farm. If this were done then the tenant might either keep ; it himself or he might let it to another : and in mai case the tenmt would have the control in his own hands, asi it would put an end on all such farms to the rabbit gnieoancei and it would also put a I stop to the annoyance of periodical visits from gangs of poachers prowling on his lands in the night. Corning to the broad question of existing relation, between I landlord a 1 tenant. Mr. Slater says the Law of Dishes, is I called a ,rd's Law. It certainly gives the lanlord a decided ml but i• in Seidant thought of in practice. I know that some large landowners in this county never take such an advantage, and they have no wish to uphold the present law. I hove known tenants to get into trouble, and the landlord hm men aide to throw a shield over them and to protect them until they could recover themmlves. I have mt time to go further into this matter, but perhaps mme of our friends will ded with the sAject more fully on some future opportunity. There is. however, another question as between landlord and fen con that is of pressing importance, end which I must not omit. We all know that the agr,cul- tural interest in far more important than any other in, rat in this country. We have an ever-increasing population which must be fed, and it would be an immense advantage to us m a nation if we could be self-supporting and feed our own peoolo. Every obstacle ought to be removed And every emmuraßement given for the better cultivation of the soil. "The Agricultural Holdings Act" was well meant, and was a fair instalment of what was neresatry ; but unfortunately it contained within itself the elements of ito own destruction. The permissive clause operated to draw all the life and blood out of it, and it has lessened rather than increaser, mutual confidence. It seems mmewhat remark- able that the very men who took part in passing the measure should at once have taken step. to defeat it. effect and to render it abortive. I think that the suspicion which at that time lurked in the minds of many landlords passed away, and if the Government were to propose to re- enact the identical Act Omitting, the fatal clause) I do not think that it would now meet with such strong eppoeition Some landlords now wish that they hail mbrnitted to its provisions. They see their reasonableness. The re-enact- ment of the Act (with the exception named) would he accepted as a valuable inAtalmmt and moult tend to remote confidence fete not think that either of our great political parties deserve many thanks from the agricultural intermits There are vital matter, at ,take. and now is the time for drawing general attention to the aubject. We hare candi- dates now in the field, and now is the Pale to quesdion them, and to elicit their opinions, and they might be asked their opinion of the Act referred to, and whether they would support its re-enactment. omitting the abortive rheum I merely suggeet them thoughts for the ronetderation of the Chamber I but I hope we shall not forget that this question. like all others, has two sides to it. Roth sidm should be looked at in a just and fair spirit.. and with an impartial eye: and while.we are devising means to secure and protect the enema most not forget the other. Cases of damage to farmers and depreciation sometimes happen, and it some- times happens that there is no remedy. If this Chamber cm asl,st in laying down better defined

1i..., and can aid in clearing away all doubt and auspicion on this subject aod in making the relation betwen landlord and tenant more harmonious and better understood it wdi do a good work and (as the French tiitYl t. iil .bserve well of the country. We should try to tube, broad view of all these questions, and not to forget that while the land is the protierty of the landlord it must (as Lord Cairns Edit us) be looked at as Affecting the in_ tereats of the country, just as our railways while they are the property of Vae shareholders exist for the good of the country—neither the one nor the other conld be handed over to ahen purposes—we cannot make our 1.04 1,00 forests and wastes, wor ,nr railways into racecourses—they exist for the good of tho coutary and we most consider them in that umst also consider no boom will avail the farmer unless it be followed up by the most untiring industry nod skill. The success of a fanner does not depend even on draining or manuring, however general and howevor The real secrit success consists in practical knowledge on all points, judicious and economical management, skill in buy- ing and selling, constant and perxnal supervision, .watch- fool eye by day and night, and a detertninatioo to make things answer. Mr. Stater abstained from all political matters in the paper read, but intitnated that be would carry the subject further at. future time.

The following words spoken by Mr. Gladstone at Marylebone convey a waggm load of truth —••I cannot Icy my hand on a good iticasure which I peeved with any mai/nonce from the Tory party; but I can lay I my hand MI many a good meaaure which, became I i happened to tread upon the toes of a few, 1 I was compelled to withdraw by the immediate readi- j sem of the Tory party to coalesce with mybody and I everybody if they could but defeat the Government." I These few words, coupled with the conclusive evi- dem. of their truth, should carry conviction to the mind of every working man that his interests am closely and uumistakably indentified with the me- mos of the Liberal party.

It should oot be forgotten that the Tories raised an outcry against the Liberals when the latter Curt nented to reftr the ALtbatna question, which almost threatened to plunge us into war with Amerina, to the decision of a tribunal composed of distinguished persons. The tribunal give their award in favour of America, and we had to pay a considerable sum of money as c,inpennation for the losses the Alabama and other privateers had oecasioned. But the Tories uontended that the honour and dignity of the reentry bad Lain saerifleed likeause it did not enter headlong into a oonflict, that would certainly have proven a terrible if not a disastrous war, in order to uphold what the other nations of Europe proclaimed to he a bad and a wndigful cause. The Afghan and Zulu MIN ware both wrong and cruel.

Apropos of the "oaf," Mr. Chamberlain asked Major Burnaby at Birmingham to explain why, if it is good to dog woldiers, it is not also good to eo.! officers Major Burnaby doesn't like the question—which is very natural—but on Thurnlav night he tried to amwer it. Ilia answer is this: • If an Englidt racer is found drunk at his Post, or com- mits an act it insubordination in the face of the enemy, Mere is no alternative for that man—he is shot. Ikt the British ruddier he the alterative of 25 lashes. This is an evasion. Drunkenness on duty and insubordination are not . the only offencee for which private soldiers on foreign ser- vice son be flogged. Under the new Act passed by this Government there is scarcely an offence for which this punishment may not be indicted; offences for which officers ars not shot, as Major Burnaby says, but mishiered—that is, Cannoned from the service. 'I here 19 thus one law for the officer and another law for the private euldier. The officer may be merely dismissed the soldier must be disgraced and brutalised by an inhuman punishment. A pasaage from one of Mr. Cross'e speeches, translated by ! the tihorthand writer mot wear mot as it fell from thr right I hon. gentleman's lips, supplies an exquisite 'menu., of the oratorical achievements of the Minister who prides himself on his ability to speak plain English end to make himself I clearly understood. It runs as follows :—But when people I eay nothing 11.18 been done my anew, at once is this : What ' has been done in Birmingham ? what is being done in ! ILondon? because before the end of next year upwards of , 12,000 of the artisans still be inhabited in the best of housen. I insteal of living in the most miserable rookeries which could possibly have exiated. But toy charge against those ' who say a word against the Act, and Mr. Bright is one of ' them, all that was explained in the House of Commons, be- I , cause we had to bring it before Erin in the eau of expen- I diture on a loan, and Mr. Bright must have known that lor ought to have know that, when he stated publicly I that not an artisin had been housed, when he must I have known, or ought to have known, that pre- visions had been taken which would have eecured before the end of MI M the metropolis alone more than , 12,0)0 people being inhabited in the best possible houses. I Thin classic utterance formed part of Mr. Cross's oration at Waterloo on 'Tuesday evening. The reader will notice how, when Mr. Bright gots into a Conservative Minister's head, all grammar immediately gets out of it. The Home Sec.. Wary embwked upon this wonderful sententh with the evident intention of levelling a crushing charge at thoee who premium " to say a word" against the Artisan,' Dwel- lings Act. Unfortunately, at a critical moment in the con.. atruction of the perial it occurred to Mr. thou that Mr. Bright 00.0 one of them ;" and all hope that the Home Secretary would emerge from this particular utterance with- out any serious V 101441011 of the rules of syntax had to be I forthwith abandoned. From thst motnent, Mr. Croon became etricken with 0 sort of 'oratorical apoplexy. Ile Eat more to say about Mr. Bright than he , ! could possibly compress into any respecMbly constructed sentence. In this contingency, the right hon. gentleman treated syntax with disdain ; and gave vent to his feelings inn plethoric outbreak of tnisplaced conjunctions and din- , connected adverbs 'rid, specimen, it must be added, is not , afar-fetched illustration of the eccentricitiee of the right ' hon.gentlenum's stele. The political student who makes Isis had ache in trying to muter the mazes of Sir Stafford Northcote's finance deserves to lie called when his fate in compared to that of the school boy condemned to parse one of Mr. Cross's sentences. The cry of " Beer mid Bible" was happily illustrated at the thirston Tory demonstration on I Saturd'ay, when arope with a quantity of bunting was tied to Garston Old Church on the one side, and to a large public.house on the other. This spectecle of a public-house supporting the Church, and the Church eupporting the pub- lic-house in a demonstration of respect for the represent.. lives of a Government which has impartially distributed its affection. between Gunpowder,Glory, Gin, and the Gospel was onrikingly illustrative of the sort of acquaintanceswhich are scraped together under the demoralising Bfluences of Ipolitical adversity.

Ma. GLADSTON• IN MIDLOTHIAN. Mr. Gladstone on Thursday addressed • great public meeting at Bormyrigg, eight miles from Edinburgh. The right hon. gentleman mid that the election. of Wednesday seemed to indicate that the nation was aware of its responsibility, and intended to do it. duty a. became a self-governing people, heir to great traditions, and bound to and on to their children of the present generation a lot as bright and as distinguished In the I world as we had inherited from those who went before us. He believed it would be found that the irreversible judge- ment of the nation would be in favour of liberty, honour, and jmike, as against a system which woe neither liberty, not justice, nor honour. The declaration of the people of England would, be was aure, he re-echoed in every vale of Scotlmd. TiOYINATION OF MR GLADSTONE AT MIDLOTHIAN.— The nomination of Mr. Gladstone and Lord Dalkeith took plane on Wednesday morning in Edinburgh without any public demonstration being excited. Mr. Gladstone, re- turning from Lord Keay's at noon, visited the Corn Exchange, And met the members of the Liberal Cominiftee for Midlothian cache Scottish Liberal Club at half-past one. Within a few minutes after the declaration of the poll the news of the Liberal victory was conveyed to Mr. McMinnies. who was at the Liheril Club, and a great crowd of persons having assembled in front of the club, the newly elected member proceeded to one of the windows on the that !floor and addreased them. .

Mr. MCMINNtFS man received with the greatest enthu- siastr., and when silence had been obtained he said I Electors of Worrington,—You hove this day won a great loud noble victory by the large majority of 529. I thank I concern heartily for that victory. I bare been subjected to on insult this afternoon such as I never experienced be- fore, and such or we should feel ourselves disgraced by if we I hod offered it to Sir Gilbert Greenall. When I wen) to re- cord my vote this afternoon my friend's representative asked me to swear first ot all that I was the man j represented myself to he—(groons)—and then to swear that I bad not vetted before at this elec'ion. Do you think we should hove done that to Sir Gilbert Greenall ? (Loud cries of "No.") We ohould beet been perfectly subarned of doing anything of the kind. But. gentlemen, I there can be no doubt wbatscever that whilst we hare fought this battle with that respect due towards our oppo- nants: they have net done the same towards us, (Great

cheering.) B. we are not going to regard that. If they think it proper ts fight with filthy hands and filthy weapon, we are not going to imitate them. (Hear, hear.) If it pleases them it does not hurt us. (Hear, hear.) Now, I have never metalled to any attack that has been made upon me at this election. (Hear, hear.) tern going to reply to thorn now. (Cheers.) If there is any Mlle who has said a disreepectful word against me, or [(mused what I call unfair means, I tell him now that in regard to that, and if possible to puni.h him for that, if ever I have the opportunity of doing him a good turn I will do it. tLoud cheers.) Now that is the reply I make to those that bare used what I believe to be unfair and disrespectful means in tarrying oa this elec. Ition. Well, now. gentlemen, I have to thank you for the extraordinam- exertions which you have made in connection 1 with this contest. div.head: MID-CHESIIIRE ELECTION.
div.p: MID-CHESIIIRE ELECTION.

THE LIBERAL CANDIDATES Al NORTHWICH. , On Temlay evening, Messrs. Latlisill and Armitage, the Liberal candidates for Mitt-Cheshire, addressed a meeting in , the Drill Hall at Northwich. The hall which will seat about a thonsand pereons, was crowded to its utmost capacity long before the advertised time of the meeting, and when the candidates arrived the doors were besieged by a crowd of entered hundereds of person% Inside, the people were packed inn dense mem, and some had climbed into the windows, and even to the brackets supporting the roof. The candidates were received with loud cheers, and groans from a section of ! the meeting which had already evinced an indinaton to die- , hub the proceedings. Mr. J. T. Btananse presided, and in opening the proceeding. said he was a thorough Liberal— (hisses and cheemo—but be did not object to a spirited foreign policy. t Loud cheers.) He did not care how spirited , a policy W. ,10 long as it was straightforward and honest— (groans, Lim, and loud cheere,)—but it cut him to the heart when he found that a represenmtive of the English Goverment had been saying one thing in public and writing an altogether different thing in private. (Cheers, hisses, and , interruption.) He described in detail, amid considerable • uproar, the policy which lied been pursued by , the Government with a view of securing the integrity of Turkey, and remarked that the Eastern question was not , yet by any means settled. The Turkish empire was in the . , throe, of dissolution, and ere long some other power would , take its place. He fervently hoped that when that time . came the voice of England would once more be heard on , the side of freedom. (Groans and loud cheers.) He next , touched upon several points of home policy, and said the , formers lied hod a feeling that the Liberal party looked I , especially after the interests of manufacturers, whilst the , iTory party were the real friends of the agricaltu -al classes. He thought that feeling was now dispelled, and he hoped to , , see a triumph of principles at this election. (Load cheers ' and groans l—Whilst the chairman had been speaking. con- I , sidemble interruption was caused by a number of young , men who. unable to obtain admission, had climbed upon the iron roof of the building, and, opening the skylight% looked , down upon the meeting. At frequent intervals they raised " cheers and groan% which were answered frotn the meeting.. ; In the meantime Mr I athain left the meeting, and addressed a large crowd outside. where he met with a very good recep- ', tion.—When order had been somewhat restored in the hall, Mr. ARNITAOR, who was loudly cheered, addressed the meeting. He commenced by referring to the domestic legislation of the Governtnent, and said that no measure of • first-rate importance had found its won' into the statute bcok since they had been in power. bt those eecond-raM . measures which w,re pissed a number were reactionary in 'heir character 00 10 numt,er were naseosor failures. Amongst t.os number must be included the Agricultural Holdings I Bill, which was introduced avowedly to fulfil the pledges . which the Government had given to the farmer.. The I celebrated 481 h section of that Act undid all the pmisible good which the Act contained. and they knew well that all , the Cheshire landowners has mken advantage of that nection, 4 and had con- .oral themselves oat of the responsibilities which the tel Laid upon them. Excepting Mr. Wilbraham Egerton, Ike thought there was not one man in the whole of , Cheshire who did not know that that Act had turneel•ut failure, as it was intended to do from the very beginning. I Another jinn, was the Artisans' Dwelling. Act, which was •, paned apparemly with the intention of providing better , houses for the working classes in the boroughs. Like the • Agricultural Holdings Bill it was a permisaive measure. and I that was one of the principal causes of its failure. What good there was in it was destroyed by its permissive ohne- , acter. Then it only referred to towns with a populatinn nt 1 more than twetly-ire thousand inhabitants, and he main- tained that any measure which had for its object the im- • . movement of the sanitary conditions of life amongst the working dames should hare • more extended action and not stop short at a few of the largest towns. (Loud cheers.)— . Mr. LATHAM subsesnently addressed the meeting, and a , resolMion in support of the candidates was adopted.
